To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the carboxylate ligand of a diiron oxygenase is shifted from bidentate to monodental upon substrate binding, which regulates the reactivity of the enzyme with dioxygen.
the diiron β-hydroxylase catalytic cycle of the chloramphenicol biosynthetic enzyme CmlA is regulated by the NRPS CmlP.
the active site of the nonheme β-hydroxylase, CmlA, is a diiron center that is reduced to a diferrous state (termed WTR).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biosynthesis of the antibiotic chloramphenicol, which is produced by Streptomyces venezuelae.
the elucidation of the structure and mechanism of action of the nonheme iron monooxygenase enzyme CmlA.
the mechanism and regulation of the first reaction in the biosynthesis of the important antibiotic chloramphenicol.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the carboxylate of E377 is a key regulatory ligand that controls dioxygen reactivity and catalytic activity of the CmlP-CmlA system.
a carboxylate shifts in response to binding of a substrate, which regulates dioxygen activation in a diiron nonheme β-hydroxylase.
the carboxylate of the amino acid residue E377 of CmlA is bidentately bound in the WTR state and monodentately bound in the CmlA:WTR:CmlPAT complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have solved the crystal structure of CmlA in the diferrous form, and we have shown that the carboxylate group of a conserved glutamate residue in the active site is responsible for regulation of dioxygen activation in this enzyme.
the carboxylate of the E377 residue in CmlA plays a critical role in regulating dioxygen activation by the diiron nonheme β-hydroxylase.

the carboxylate of Glu377 regulates dioxygen activation by CmlA upon binding of a substrate-loaded CmlP, and that the carboxylic acid group of the substrate is essential for hydroxylation of the substrate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a novel mechanism of regulating dioxygen activation in diiron non-heme oxygenases.

the active site of a diiron non-heme monooxygenase is regulated by a carboxylate that is shifted from bidentate to monodendate coordination in the presence of the non-ribosomal peptide synthase to which the substrate is bound.
the active site of the diiron β-hydroxylase is in a high-spin, coordinatively saturated state in the absence of substrate.
